In Linear Algebra 00 a matrix was only a compact way to write a system of equations. This post treats matrices as objects with their own algebra: they can be added, multiplied, transposed and — sometimes — inverted. Matrix multiplication is the operation that makes all of this interesting, so it gets four separate readings, each useful in a different situation. Then row operations become matrices themselves (elementary matrices), which turns Gaussian elimination into an algebraic statement: A=LU, a lower triangular matrix times an upper triangular one, or PA=LU when rows must be exchanged. This factorization is how real software solves Ax=b, and it explains a rule every numerical programmer learns early: do not compute A−1 to solve a linear system.

m×n matrix — a rectangular array of numbers with m rows and n columns. aij is the entry in row i, column j.
Square matrix — m=n. Its main diagonal is a11,a22,…,ann.
Identity matrix In — square, 1 on the main diagonal, 0 elsewhere. Inx=x for all x.
Zero matrix 0 — all entries 0.
Equal matrices — same size and the same entry in every position.
Addition and scalar multiplication work entry by entry, exactly as for vectors, and obey the same eight rules. Only matrices of the same size can be added.

If A is m×n and B is n×p, the product AB is the m×p matrix with entries
(AB)ij=∑k=1naikbkj=ai1b1j+ai2b2j+⋯+ainbnj.
The inner sizes must match: (m×n)(n×p)=m×p. The example used throughout this chapter:
A=(1234),B=(5678),AB=(19224350).

1. Entry by entry (row times column). (AB)ij is the dot product of row i of A with column j of B. For example (AB)12=1⋅6+2⋅8=22.
2. By columns. Column j of AB is A times column j of B:
AB=A(b1⋯bp)=(Ab1⋯Abp).
So every column of AB is a combination of the columns of A. Here Ab1=5(1,3)+7(2,4)=(19,43).
3. By rows. Row i of AB is row i of A times B, so every row of AB is a combination of the rows of B. Here row 1 is 1⋅(5,6)+2⋅(7,8)=(19,22). This is the view that explains elimination: row operations combine rows.
4. Columns times rows (sum of outer products). Multiply column k of A (an m×1 matrix) by row k of B (a 1×p matrix). Each such product is a full m×p matrix of rank at most one (Linear Algebra 02), and AB is their sum:
AB=∑k=1nakbk∗=(13)(56)+(24)(78)=(561518)+(14162832)=(19224350).
Here bk∗ denotes row k of B. This view reappears in the SVD (Linear Algebra 05), which writes a matrix as a sum of rank-one pieces ordered by importance.
All four give the same numbers because each one computes ∑kaikbkj in position (i,j); they only group the work differently.
Trick: pick the view that matches the question. "Is b in the column space?" — columns. "What does a row operation do?" — rows. "What is the rank of AB?" — outer products. "Just give me a number" — entries.

For matrices of compatible sizes:
A(BC)=(AB)C (associative), A(B+C)=AB+AC and (A+B)C=AC+BC (distributive), c(AB)=(cA)B=A(cB), and ImA=A=AIn.
Proof of associativity. For a vector x, Bx=∑kxkbk, so A(Bx)=∑kxkAbk=(AB)x by the column view. Apply this to each column cj of C: column j of A(BC) is A(Bcj)=(AB)cj, which is column j of (AB)C. ■
Three rules from ordinary algebra fail:
Not commutative. BA=(23343146)≠AB. (Often only one of AB, BA is even defined.)
Zero divisors. With N=(0100), N≠0 but N2=0.
No cancellation. AB=AC does not imply B=C, even when A≠0 (take A=N, B=N, C=0).
Common pitfall: (A+B)2=A2+AB+BA+B2, not A2+2AB+B2. The two agree only when AB=BA.

The transpose AT of an m×n matrix is the n×m matrix with (AT)ij=aji: rows become columns. Rules:
(AT)T=A,(A+B)T=AT+BT,(cA)T=cAT,(AB)T=BTAT.
Proof of the last rule. ((AB)T)ij=(AB)ji=∑kajkbki=∑k(BT)ik(AT)kj=(BTAT)ij. ■
The order reverses, just like taking off shoes and socks. The dot product is a matrix product: x⋅y=xTy (a 1×1 matrix).

Type · Definition · Useful facts
Diagonal · aij=0 for i≠j · products and powers act entry by entry on the diagonal
Upper triangular · aij=0 for i>j · product of two upper triangular is upper triangular
Lower triangular · aij=0 for i<j · same for lower; unit lower triangular has 1s on the diagonal
Symmetric · AT=A · ATA and AAT are always symmetric
Permutation · the rows of I in some order · P ⁣A reorders the rows of A; P−1=PT
ATA is symmetric: (ATA)T=AT(AT)T=ATA. For example, with X=(123456), XTX=(35444456). This matrix is the heart of least squares (Linear Algebra 05).
Product of lower triangular matrices is lower triangular. If aik=0 for k>i and bkj=0 for j>k, then in (AB)ij=∑kaikbkj a term can be nonzero only if j≤k≤i. When i<j there is no such k, so (AB)ij=0. If both have unit diagonal, (AB)ii=aiibii=1. ■
Permutation matrices. Each row and each column of P has exactly one 1. The rows of P are orthonormal, so PPT=I, which means P−1=PT.

A matrix can be cut by horizontal and vertical lines into blocks (submatrices). If the column cuts of A match the row cuts of B, then AB can be computed block by block, using the same formula as for numbers — but keeping the order of each product:
(A11A12A21A22)(B11B12B21B22)=(A11B11+A12B21A11B12+A12B22A21B11+A22B21A21B12+A22B22).
The four views of Chapter 1 are all special cases: the column view cuts B into columns, the row view cuts A into rows, and the outer-product view cuts A into columns and B into rows.

Let M=(ABCD) with A square and invertible. Eliminating the block C is one block row operation — "block row 2 minus CA−1 times block row 1":
(I0−CA−1I)(ABCD)=(AB0D−CA−1B).
The block S=D−CA−1B is the Schur complement of A in M. When every block is 1×1 this is exactly one step of ordinary elimination: d−(c/a)b. Schur complements appear in statistics (conditional covariance), in optimization and in domain-decomposition solvers.
Watch out: in block formulas every product must keep its order. CA−1B cannot be rewritten as A−1BC or BCA−1.

An elementary matrix is the result of one row operation on the identity. Multiplying A on the left by E performs that row operation on A (by the row view: row i of EA is row i of E times A).
Using the 3×3 system from Linear Algebra 00,
A=(121381041),E21=(100−310001),E32=(1000100−21).
E21 subtracts 3 times row 1 from row 2; E32 subtracts 2 times row 2 from row 3. (No E31 is needed because a31 is already 0.) Then
E32E21A=(12102−2005)=U.
Every elementary matrix is invertible, and its inverse is elementary of the same type: undo "subtract ℓ times row j" by "add ℓ times row j"; undo a swap by the same swap; undo scaling by c by scaling by 1/c. For example
E21−1=(100310001).

E32E21=(100−3106−21),E21−1E32−1=(100310021).
The entry 6 in the first product appears because row 3 is changed using the new row 2, which already contains −3 times row 1; indeed 6=(−2)(−3). The inverses, multiplied in the opposite order, do not interact at all: the multipliers 3 and 2 simply drop into place. That clean matrix is L, and Chapter 7 is built on it. (The messy product E32E21 is L−1.)

A square n×n matrix A is invertible (or nonsingular) if there is a matrix C with
CA=IandAC=I.
Then C is called the inverse and written A−1. A square matrix without an inverse is singular.
The inverse is unique. If CA=I and AD=I, then C=CI=C(AD)=(CA)D=ID=D. ■ (This short argument even shows a left inverse and a right inverse must agree.)
Properties. If A and B are invertible n×n matrices, then
(A−1)−1=A,(AB)−1=B−1A−1,(AT)−1=(A−1)T.
Proof. (AB)(B−1A−1)=A(BB−1)A−1=AA−1=I, and similarly in the other order. For the transpose, take the transpose of AA−1=I: (A−1)TAT=I, and similarly AT(A−1)T=I. ■
If A is invertible, Ax=b has exactly one solution for every b, namely x=A−1b: it is a solution because A(A−1b)=b, and it is the only one because Ax=b implies x=A−1Ax=A−1b.

(abcd)−1=1ad−bc(d−b−ca),provided ad−bc≠0.
Proof. Multiply: (abcd)(d−b−ca)=(ad−bc00ad−bc), and the same holds in the other order. Divide by ad−bc. If ad−bc=0, the same product shows A times a matrix gives 0; Exercise 6 shows A is then singular. ■
The number ad−bc is the determinant of the 2×2 matrix (Linear Algebra 03 defines it for all sizes). For A=(1234): ad−bc=4−6=−2, so
A−1=−12(4−2−31)=(−213/2−1/2).

Why it works. Suppose row operations E1,…,Ek turn A into I: Ek⋯E1A=I. Then Ek⋯E1 is a left inverse of A, and (by the invertible matrix theorem below) it is A−1. Applying the same operations to I produces Ek⋯E1I=A−1. So: row reduce the wide matrix [ A∣I ]; if the left half becomes I, the right half is A−1. If the left half develops a zero row, A is singular.
Worked example. Take the "second difference" matrix
K=(2−10−12−10−12).
Forward elimination: R2←R2+12R1, then R3←R3+23R2:
(2−1010003/2−11/210004/31/32/31).
The pivots are 2,32,43. Backward elimination: R2←R2+34R3, then R1←R1+23R2:
(2003/211/203/203/43/23/4004/31/32/31).
Divide each row by its pivot:
K−1=(3/41/21/41/211/21/41/23/4)=14(321242123).
Two observations that matter later. K is symmetric and so is K−1 (Exercise 7). And K is tridiagonal — mostly zeros — but K−1 is completely full. Keep that in mind for Chapter 8.

Theorem. For a square n×n matrix A, the following are equivalent (all true or all false):
A is invertible.
A is row equivalent to In.
A has n pivot positions.
Ax=0 has only the trivial solution.
The columns of A are linearly independent.
Ax=b has at least one solution for every b∈Rn.
The columns of A span Rn.
There is an n×n matrix C with CA=I.
There is an n×n matrix D with AD=I.
AT is invertible.
A is a product of elementary matrices.
Proof. (1) ⇒ (8) and (1) ⇒ (9): take C=D=A−1.
(8) ⇒ (4): if Ax=0 then x=CAx=C0=0.
(4) ⇔ (5): this is the definition of independence (Linear Algebra 00, Chapter 8).
(4) ⇒ (3): only the trivial solution means no free variables, so every one of the n columns is a pivot column.
(3) ⇒ (2): n pivots in an n×n matrix means one pivot in every row and every column, on the diagonal, so the RREF is In.
(2) ⇒ (11): Ek⋯E1A=I gives A=E1−1⋯Ek−1, a product of elementary matrices.
(11) ⇒ (1): elementary matrices are invertible, and so is any product of invertible matrices.
(9) ⇒ (6): given b, the vector x=Db satisfies Ax=ADb=b.
(6) ⇔ (7): Ax ranges over all combinations of the columns (Linear Algebra 00).
(6) ⇒ (3): if A had fewer than n pivots, its echelon form U would have a zero last row. Choose c with last entry 1; then Ux=c is inconsistent, and undoing the row operations on c gives a b with Ax=b inconsistent, contradicting (6).

(1) ⇔ (10): if A is invertible, (A−1)T inverts AT (Chapter 5); apply this to AT for the converse.
Every statement is now linked to every other. ■
Corollary (one-sided is enough). If A and B are square and AB=I, then BA=I and B=A−1. Proof: AB=I is statement (9) for A, so A is invertible; multiply AB=I on the left by A−1 to get B=A−1. ■
Watch out: the corollary needs square matrices. For A=(10) and B=(10), AB=(1)=I1 but BA=(1000)≠I2.
Linear Algebra 02, 03 and 04 add more lines to this list: rank n, null space {0}, det⁡A≠0, and 0 is not an eigenvalue.

Suppose elimination on A needs no row exchanges. Then only replacement operations "row i minus ℓij times row j" (with i>j) are used, and
(E32E31E21) A=U⟹A=(E21−1E31−1E32−1) U=LU
(written for n=3; larger n is the same). U is upper triangular with the pivots on its diagonal. L is unit lower triangular, and as Chapter 4 showed, its entries below the diagonal are exactly the multipliers: Lij=ℓij.
For the running example, the multipliers were ℓ21=3, ℓ31=0, ℓ32=2, so
(121381041)=(100310021)(12102−2005).
Multiply it out to check: row 2 of LU is 3(1,2,1)+(0,2,−2)=(3,8,1), and row 3 is 2(0,2,−2)+(0,0,5)=(0,4,1).

Ax=b becomes L(Ux)=b. Put c=Ux and solve two triangular systems:
Forward substitution Lc=b (top to bottom).
Back substitution Ux=c (bottom to top).
With b=(2,12,2): c1=2; 3c1+c2=12 gives c2=6; 2c2+c3=2 gives c3=−10. So c=(2,6,−10) — exactly the right-hand side that elimination produced in Linear Algebra 00. Then Ux=c gives z=−2, y=1, x=2, as before.
The point: the factorization is done once; each new right-hand side then costs only two cheap triangular solves.

Divide each row of U by its pivot to get A=LDU′ with D the diagonal matrix of pivots and U′ unit upper triangular. For the example, D=diag⁡(1,2,5) and
U′=(12101−1001).
When A is symmetric and has an LU factorization, U′=LT, so A=LDLT. For a symmetric matrix with all pivots positive this becomes the Cholesky factorization A=(LD1/2)(LD1/2)T, which costs about half as much as LU.

Theorem. If A is invertible and A=L1U1=L2U2 with L1,L2 unit lower triangular and U1,U2 upper triangular, then L1=L2 and U1=U2.
Proof. Since A is invertible, so are the Ui (and the unit-diagonal Li always are). From L1U1=L2U2,
L2−1L1=U2U1−1.
The left side is unit lower triangular (inverses and products of unit lower triangular matrices are unit lower triangular — Chapter 2 and Exercise 5), and the right side is upper triangular. A matrix that is both is diagonal, and its diagonal is all 1s from the left side. So both sides equal I, which gives L1=L2 and U1=U2. ■

Elimination breaks down when a zero appears in a pivot position. Example:
A=(011121279).
The (1,1) entry is 0, so swap rows 1 and 2 first. If all the exchanges are done at the start, they form one permutation matrix P, and PA factors without further trouble:
P=(010100001),PA=(121011279)=(100010231)(121011004).
The multipliers were ℓ21=0, ℓ31=2 (row 3 becomes (0,3,7)), then ℓ32=3 (row 3 becomes (0,0,4)).
Theorem. For every invertible A there is a permutation matrix P such that PA=LU with L unit lower triangular and U upper triangular with nonzero pivots. An invertible A has an LU factorization with no exchanges (P=I) exactly when every leading principal submatrix (the top-left k×k block, k=1,…,n) is invertible.
To solve Ax=b from PA=LU: LUx=Pb, so permute b, then do the two triangular solves.
Common pitfall: after factoring PA=LU, forgetting to apply P to b. The factorization is of PA, not of A.

A flop is one floating-point add, subtract, multiply or divide. At elimination step k of an n×n matrix, each of the n−k rows below the pivot needs one division (its multiplier) and a multiply and a subtract for each of the remaining n−k entries. So step k costs (n−k)(2(n−k)+1) flops, and in total
∑k=1n(2(n−k)2+(n−k))=23n3−12n2−16n≈23n3.
Each triangular solve costs about n2 flops. So for n=1000: roughly 6.7×108 flops to factor, then only about 2×106 per right-hand side.

Speed. Forming A−1 costs about 2n3 flops — roughly three times the LU factorization — and then A−1b still costs 2n2, the same as the two triangular solves it was supposed to replace. There is nothing to gain even with many right-hand sides, because LU is reusable too.
Accuracy. Gaussian elimination with partial pivoting is backward stable in practice: the computed x exactly solves a system with a very slightly perturbed A. Multiplying by a computed inverse does not have this guarantee in general, and its residual ∥b−Ax∥ is typically larger (Higham, Chapters 9 and 14).
Structure. A banded or sparse matrix has banded or sparse LU factors (without pivoting, a tridiagonal K has bidiagonal L and U), but its inverse is usually full — as K−1 in Chapter 5 showed. For large sparse problems the inverse may not even fit in memory.
In code this means numpy.linalg.solve(A, b) (which calls LAPACK's LU-based gesv), or scipy.linalg.lu_factor once and lu_solve for each right-hand side — never inv(A) @ b.
Trick: read A−1b in a formula as "the solution of Ax=b", not as an instruction to invert. The same holds for expressions like A−1B (solve with many right-hand sides) and cTA−1b (one solve, then one dot product).

Let A=(1021) and B=(3102). Compute AB and BA. Describe AB with the row view.
Solution
AB=(3164) and BA=(5142), which differ. Row view: A is an elementary matrix ("add 2 times row 1 to row 2"), so AB is B with row 2 replaced by (0,2)+2(3,1)=(6,4).

Prove (ABC)T=CTBTAT, and deduce that BTAB is symmetric whenever A is symmetric.
Solution
(ABC)T=((AB)C)T=CT(AB)T=CTBTAT. If AT=A, then (BTAB)T=BTAT(BT)T=BTAB.

Find the inverse of (2513) with the 2×2 formula, and of (123014560) by Gauss–Jordan.
Solution
ad−bc=6−5=1, so the first inverse is (3−5−12).
For the 3×3 matrix, row reducing [ A∣I ] gives
A−1=(−2418520−15−4−541).
Check one entry of AA−1: row 3 of A times column 1 of A−1 is 5(−24)+6(20)+0=0, as it should be.

Show that the inverse of a unit lower triangular matrix is unit lower triangular (this completes the uniqueness proof in Chapter 7).
Solution
A unit lower triangular L reduces to I using only operations "row i minus a multiple of row j" with i>j (no swaps, no scaling, since the pivots are already 1). Each such elementary matrix is unit lower triangular, so L−1, the product of these elementary matrices, is unit lower triangular by the Chapter 2 result.

Show that if ad−bc=0 then A=(abcd) is singular. Also show that (0111) is invertible but has no LU factorization without a row exchange.
Solution
If A=0 it is singular. Otherwise M=(d−b−ca)≠0 and AM=0. If A were invertible, M=A−1AM=0, a contradiction.
For the second matrix, ad−bc=−1≠0, so it is invertible. If (0111)=(10ℓ1)(u11u120u22), the (1,1) entry forces u11=0, but then the (2,1) entry is ℓu11=0≠1. Its first leading principal submatrix (0) is singular, as the theorem predicts. With the swap, PA=(1101)=I⋅U.

Prove: if A is symmetric and invertible, then A−1 is symmetric.
Solution
(A−1)T=(AT)−1=A−1, using the transpose rule for inverses from Chapter 5 and AT=A.

Linear Algebra 02 steps back from matrices to the structures they act on. It defines a vector space by axioms (so polynomials, functions and matrices count), then subspaces, span, independence, basis and dimension — with a full proof that dimension is well defined (the Steinitz exchange lemma). It then studies the four fundamental subspaces of a matrix, proves that row rank equals column rank, and proves rank–nullity in matrix form.
